sections.h: A worked example of naming by purpose
sections.flag: Illustrative: my own sketch, not a sourced fact.
p: Same screen, two vocabularies. Suppose a model is asked to add a delete confirmation. Given red-500 and gray-100, it has to guess what each is for, and a guess that looks fine will pass review. Given text-danger and surface-raised, the choice is mostly made by the names. The model is selecting a purpose, not inventing a style.

The error changes shape. With primitives, a wrong pick is a wrong color, which is hard to spot and hard to grep for. With semantic names, a wrong pick is a wrong purpose, such as using a danger token for a warning. That is still a mistake, but it is the kind a reviewer can read in the code and reason about in one pass.

sections.h: What I would do first on a real product
sections.flag: My opinion, based on the tradeoffs above.
p: Audit the names before the values. I would list every token a generator could reach and ask of each one whether its name says when to use it. Anything named after how it looks, not what it does, is a candidate for renaming or hiding. This costs an afternoon and needs no new tooling.

Hide primitives last, not first. Removing access in one step could break existing flows that quietly depend on raw values. I would first make the semantic layer complete enough that nothing needs the primitives, then close the door. If a flow still reaches for one, that gap in the vocabulary is useful information about what is missing.

sections.h: Where I would not trust this yet
sections.flag: My opinion, based on the tradeoffs above.
p: A thin semantic layer pushes people back. If the vocabulary is missing a purpose someone really needs, they will find a way around it, and the model will too. Hiding primitives only works if the semantic set is generous enough to cover real work. I would not claim the safety benefit without checking that.

Names can drift. A token called action-primary that is used for three unrelated things has the same problem as blue-500, just better dressed. I would treat the intent notes as part of the token, reviewed when the token changes, not as optional documentation.
